bull_thesis:
The bull case is that a dated, well-supported regulatory decision on 22 December 2026 turns Mineralys from a clinical-stage company into the owner of a commercial cardiovascular drug, and that the market has marked the shares down for the wrong reason.

Start with the event. The United States Food and Drug Administration accepted the filing for lorundrostat in March 2026 and set a decision date of 22 December 2026. That date has been reconfirmed in company releases on 6 May and 14 June 2026 and has not moved. No advisory committee meeting has been called, which is normally a sign the agency does not think it needs outside help with the risk-benefit question. The filing rests on two registrational studies, the Phase 3 Launch-HTN trial and the Phase 2 Advance-HTN trial, both showing clinically meaningful reductions in systolic blood pressure on top of existing therapy, within a body of five completed successful Phase 2/3 trials.

The strongest single piece of evidence for approval is external. On 18 May 2026 the same agency approved AstraZeneca's baxdrostat, sold as Baxfendy, as the first aldosterone synthase inhibitor for adults with inadequately controlled high blood pressure. Aldosterone synthase is the enzyme that makes aldosterone, the hormone that raises blood pressure and damages the heart and kidneys over time; lorundrostat blocks the same enzyme. The regulator has therefore already accepted the mechanism, the blood-pressure endpoint and the safety management that goes with it, chiefly the risk of high potassium and low sodium. A second entrant with two positive registrational trials into a class the agency has just blessed is about as de-risked as a first approval gets. A reasonable probability of approval is around 90%.

The second pillar is that management has voted with real money. On 3 June 2026 Mineralys paid Tanabe $200 million in cash to extinguish the royalty on lorundrostat and to secure assignment of the related patents, funding it with $150 million of stock sold at $26.50 a share and $100 million drawn from a new senior secured loan facility of up to $500 million from Pharmakon. Boards that doubt an approval do not spend $200 million buying out a royalty on an unapproved drug at a depressed share price. Mineralys will now keep 100% of lorundrostat's future economics and own the underlying intellectual property outright, which both raises the value of a successful launch and makes the company a far cleaner acquisition target.

The third pillar is the size of the prize relative to what is priced. Bullish sell-side work sizes the aldosterone synthase inhibitor market above $5 billion and assumes a roughly even split between the two drugs. Published targets sit at $42 at Goldman Sachs and $43 at Bank of America, both buy ratings, with a consensus near $49 across roughly ten analysts against a last close of $25.52. Stripping out roughly $547 million of net cash, the market is valuing the drug itself at about $1.7 billion, which is less than one times a plausible peak-sales figure for a chronic cardiovascular medicine with patent protection.

The fourth pillar is positioning. The shares are down about 46% from a 52-week high of $47.65. Roughly 14.3% of the freely traded shares were sold short at the 15 July 2026 settlement, needing about 9.8 days of average volume to cover, and that short position has begun to shrink, falling about 14% from the prior reading. The June equity offering at $26.50 cleared a supply overhang and reset the marginal holder. An approval into that positioning has the fuel for a sharp move.

The conditions that must hold: the December date must not slip and no advisory committee may be called; the label must be broad enough to compete, ideally supported by the chronic kidney disease subgroup data presented on 30 May 2026 showing significant blood-pressure and urine-albumin reductions; and the company must not need punitive equity financing before it can show launch traction.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is that investors are buying a high-probability event whose reward is already largely in the price, while the punishment for the low-probability outcome is severe and only loosely bounded.

Begin with the payoff, not the probability. Because AstraZeneca's baxdrostat was approved on 18 May 2026 and reached the market in early June, the December decision has stopped being a question of whether the drug works and become a question of whether anyone will buy it. The approval is therefore largely expected, and an expected event does not pay much. A realistic reaction to a clean approval is a re-rate of roughly 30% to 50%, not a move to the $49 consensus target, because those targets are twelve-month launch valuations that require commercial proof Mineralys cannot deliver for a year or more. Meanwhile a rejection letter, at maybe a one-in-ten chance, would plausibly halve the shares. The shape of the payoff runs the wrong way for an event trade.

Second, the commercial case has been narrowing all year and the market noticed. The Phase 2 Explore-OSA study in obstructive sleep apnoea missed its primary goal on 10 March 2026, closing off the second indication and reducing what was pitched as a multi-disease platform to a single-drug, single-indication launch. The chronic kidney disease and heart-failure biomarker work that survived is post-hoc subgroup analysis, useful for the label and for prescribers but not an approval of its own. Bearish sell-side work argues lorundrostat is undifferentiated versus Baxfendy and structurally disadvantaged in the kidney-disease and SGLT2-combination opportunity; Goldman Sachs cut its target to $42 from $49 in June while keeping a buy rating. Being roughly seven months late to your own class against a company with a global cardiovascular sales force is a serious handicap that no amount of subgroup data fixes.

Third, the reimbursement wall. Both drugs are add-on therapies. Insurers will almost certainly require patients to fail cheap generic spironolactone, a decades-old drug that also blunts aldosterone, before paying for a branded aldosterone synthase inhibitor. That compresses both the price and the eligible volume for the entire class, and Mineralys, as the second entrant without a large contracting organisation, negotiates from the weaker position. Management has not addressed this in public materials.

Fourth, the floor is thinner than it looks. Gross cash of roughly $647 million pro forma sounds like protection until you note that the Pharmakon loan is senior secured, meaning the lender's claim ranks ahead of shareholders on the company's assets including the cash, and that the remaining three tranches of the $500 million facility carry drawdown conditions the company would likely fail in a rejection scenario. Net of the $100 million drawn, net cash is about $6.20 a share, only 24% of the $25.52 price. There is also up to $265 million of commercial milestone money still owed to Tanabe, which is a tax on the good outcome. In a rejection, holders rely not on cash but on the residual worth of a re-fileable asset, and history says that number is set by a demoralised market, not by a formula.

Fifth, the cost of winning. A branded cardiovascular launch against AstraZeneca is expensive. General and administrative spending already more than tripled to $21.0 million in the first quarter of 2026 from $6.6 million a year earlier, before a single prescription; quarterly net loss was $39.3 million and the trailing twelve-month loss about $151.8 million, and both will widen through the launch. The funding answers, the undrawn $400 million of secured debt and future equity, both cost shareholders, one in interest at the Secured Overnight Financing Rate plus 5.50% with a 3.25% floor, the other in dilution.

What would confirm the bear case: an advisory committee being called or the December date slipping; a narrow or restricted label; early prescription data showing Baxfendy taking the great majority of new starts; or a large equity raise in the first half of 2027 below today's price.

forcing_function:
The 22 December 2026 decision date is the forcing function, and it is genuinely binding: the agency must issue either an approval or a complete response letter on or about that day, and the clock is set by statute rather than by management's discretion. The stock cannot remain in its current limbo past that date.

Three things make that date unusually decisive here. First, it resolves in one stroke the only question that has kept the shares depressed since the sleep-apnoea failure in March and the competitor approval in May, namely whether Mineralys owns a commercial product at all. Second, it gates the remaining three tranches of the $500 million Pharmakon senior secured facility, whose drawdown conditions are the difference between a funded launch and a dilutive equity raise. Third, it is the gate on any strategic conversation: having paid Tanabe $200 million in June to extinguish the royalty and take assignment of the patents, Mineralys will be a wholly-owned, approved, single-asset cardiovascular company on 23 December, the cleanest possible acquisition target, at a moment when the entire class has just been validated by AstraZeneca's own approval.

Two earlier waypoints matter for timing. Second-quarter results, due in the first half of August 2026, will show the pro-forma balance sheet after the June transactions and the pace of the commercial build. And any announcement of an advisory committee meeting, or a three-month extension of the review clock, would be an immediate and serious negative; the absence of both this late in a standard review is a quiet positive that strengthens each week.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market runs in both directions, which is why this is a four rather than a five.

The market is too pessimistic on the event. The consensus reading of AstraZeneca's baxdrostat approval on 18 May 2026 was that it is bad news for Mineralys, and the shares fell about 25% in six sessions in early June to reflect it. That reading is half wrong. Competitively, yes, it is bad. Regulatorily, it is the best news Mineralys received all year: the agency has now accepted the mechanism, the blood-pressure endpoint and the safety management for this exact class. The probability that lorundrostat is approved on 22 December went up, not down, and the market marked the stock down anyway, then let it drift lower still through late July, from $26.71 to $25.52. Add that the June share sale at $26.50 was forced supply, sold to fund a royalty buyout rather than to rescue the business, and the marginal price today reflects mechanics rather than fundamentals. Roughly 14.3% of the free float remains sold short into a decision the odds favour, though that position began shrinking into the 15 July settlement.

The market is also too optimistic on the payoff, and this is the part the street will not say aloud. The consensus target near $49, with Goldman Sachs at $42 (cut from $49 in June) and Bank of America at $43 (raised from $38), is a twelve-month launch valuation. It embeds commercial share that will not be observable until well into 2027. The assumption of an even split of a $5 billion-plus market between the two drugs is a forecast, not a finding, and it is being made about a drug arriving roughly seven months late against a company with a global cardiovascular sales force. The unaddressed variable in every one of those models is reimbursement: insurers will very likely require patients to fail cheap generic spironolactone before paying for a branded aldosterone synthase inhibitor, which compresses price and eligible volume for the whole class. Nobody has priced that properly because nobody has data on it yet.

Our position is therefore that the December event is worth about $38 a share, not $49, and that this still leaves a 49% gap to the $25.52 last close. We are buying an under-priced high-probability event, not an under-priced franchise.
valley_of_death:
The risky window between now and the decision is unusually mild, which is one of the better features of this setup.

There is no funding cliff. The company held $646.1 million in cash and investments at 31 March 2026 with no debt, then transacted from a position of strength on 3 June 2026: $150 million of stock sold at $26.50, $100 million drawn on a new senior secured loan, $200 million paid out to Tanabe. Pro forma gross cash is roughly $647 million against a first-quarter net loss of $39.3 million. There is no maturity wall, since the Pharmakon loan runs to June 2031, and no covenant test that a pre-revenue company would obviously trip before December. Management's stated runway extends into 2028. The financing was done ahead of the event rather than into it, which removes the single most common way these trades go wrong.

The real hazards in the next three to nine months are informational rather than financial. First, an announcement of an advisory committee meeting or a three-month extension of the review clock. Neither has happened, and the absence of both this late in a standard review is meaningfully reassuring, but either would hit the shares hard and immediately. Second, competitive data points: AstraZeneca's Baxfendy has been available since early June 2026, so by the fourth quarter there will be early prescription trends, formulary decisions and payer policies visible for the class. If those show insurers imposing hard step-therapy through generic spironolactone, or Baxfendy locking up formulary positions before Mineralys can even file for coverage, the launch model degrades before Mineralys sells a single pill. Third, second-quarter results, due in the first half of August 2026, will show general and administrative spending continuing to climb, having already more than tripled to $21.0 million from $6.6 million a year earlier, and a widening loss, which reads badly to anyone not underwriting the launch. The stock's quiet drift lower through late July, on no company news beyond a routine hiring-grant filing on 27 July, suggests the market is already anticipating that.

The fourth hazard is the one nobody can hedge: a rejection letter. It is roughly a one-in-ten event, and it happens on a known day. There is no way to be long this name into 22 December and not own that risk. The mitigation is sizing, not cleverness.
positioning_washout:
The forced selling has largely already happened, and that is a significant part of why this is actionable now rather than in the autumn.

Three waves cleared the register in the first half of 2026. The sleep-apnoea failure on 10 March removed the platform narrative and with it the growth-oriented specialists who owned the multi-indication story. AstraZeneca's approval on 18 May removed the first-in-class premium. Then on 3 June the company itself put about 5.66 million new shares into the market at $26.50, roughly 6.4% dilution, to fund the Tanabe royalty buyout, which is the purest form of mechanical supply: stock sold for a corporate purpose, into a falling tape, with no regard for price. The shares lost about 25% over six sessions. From a 52-week high of $47.65 the stock is down about 46%.

What remains is a shareholder base fully re-priced at $26.50 and a short position of 9.55 million shares, about 14.3% of the freely traded stock at the 15 July 2026 settlement, requiring roughly 9.8 days of average volume to cover. Importantly, that reading was down about 14% from the prior settlement, which reverses the build seen through the spring: the shorts have started to trim ahead of the date. A position of that size into a scheduled, statutory decision has a characteristic behaviour: it must either be covered before the date or carried through it, and the cost of carrying rises as the date approaches and options premiums inflate. Either path is a source of demand into December.

One caution against reading this as pure fuel. The buyers of the June offering at $26.50 are underwater and unlikely to add. And the reason the short interest exists is not irrational: it is a legitimate bet that a second-to-market drug in a class dominated by a large competitor will disappoint commercially. Those shorts do not need the December decision to go their way; they need 2027 prescription data to go their way. A washout in the shareholder base is not, by itself, a thesis.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a buy now, sized as a defined-odds bet rather than a defined-risk one, and that distinction is exactly what holds the conviction at four instead of five.

The setup is genuine and it has been re-verified today. There is a hard, statutory, dated event: the United States Food and Drug Administration must decide on lorundrostat, Mineralys's once-daily blood-pressure pill, on or about 22 December 2026, now 141 days away. The date has not moved since it was set in March and has been restated by the company as recently as 14 June. No advisory committee has been called. The filing rests on two registrational trials within five successful Phase 2/3 studies. And most importantly, on 18 May 2026 the same agency approved AstraZeneca's baxdrostat, which blocks the identical enzyme for the identical patients, meaning the regulator has already accepted the mechanism, the endpoint and the safety profile of this class. A second entrant into a freshly validated class, with a clean review and no committee, is about a nine-in-ten proposition.

Management has staked real money on the same view. In June it paid Tanabe $200 million cash to extinguish the royalty on a drug that is not yet approved and to take assignment of the patents, funded with $150 million of stock at $26.50 and $100 million of a new $500 million senior secured facility. Nobody does that at a depressed price if they expect a rejection letter. It also leaves Mineralys, on 23 December, as a wholly-owned, approved, single-asset cardiovascular company, the cleanest acquisition target imaginable in a class a major pharmaceutical company has just proven out.

The price has been washed out for reasons that are only half about the fundamentals, and it has drifted lower again in the past week, to $25.52 from $26.71, on no company news. The shares are down about 46% from a 52-week high of $47.65, with about 14.3% of the free float sold short, though that short position is now shrinking rather than growing. Some of the decline is legitimate: the sleep-apnoea study failed its primary endpoint in March, which killed the platform story. Some of it is mechanical: a forced 6.4% equity issue in June into a falling tape. Against a street consensus target near $49, with Goldman Sachs at $42 and Bank of America at $43, the gap is real.

Now the honest part. Two of the three legs a top-conviction event trade requires are here; the third is not.

First, the payoff is not the wide asymmetry this funnel exists to find. Because the competitor was approved in May, the approval is expected, and expected events do not pay much. A clean approval is worth perhaps a 30% to 50% move, to roughly $38, not to the $49 consensus, which is a twelve-month launch valuation requiring commercial proof that will not exist until deep into 2027. A rejection letter roughly halves the stock. So the shape is +49% against -49%, about one to one. It is the odds that make this work, since 0.90 x $38 plus 0.10 x $13 gives a base-case value near $35.50, or +39% from here, not the ratio. The July drift has improved that ratio slightly, which is the one thing that changed for the better in the last week.

Second, and this is the binding constraint, the downside floor is soft. There is no deal price, no contractual payout, no cash backstop near the market. Gross cash of roughly $647 million looks like protection until you note the Pharmakon loan is senior secured, so the lender ranks ahead of shareholders on the company's assets including that cash, and that the remaining three tranches carry conditions a rejected company would fail. Net cash is about $6.20 a share, just 24% of the price. The realistic $13 support level is our estimate of where a re-fileable asset in an already-approved class would clear, corroborated only by where the stock traded a year ago before the pivotal data. That is a judgement, not a floor, and it is why the margin-of-safety score is a two while the event score is a four.

The timing call: enter now rather than waiting. The reason is asymmetric information flow between here and December. The two things that would break the thesis, an advisory committee being called or the review clock being extended, get less likely with every week that passes this late in a standard review, while the reward for owning the position does not improve by waiting. Second-quarter results in the first half of August will show a widening loss and a heavier commercial build, and may offer a marginally better entry, but that is a coin-flip against the risk of the shorts continuing to cover into the autumn.

Size it accordingly: a full-conviction thesis at half-conviction size. Underwrite as though roughly half the capital is genuinely at risk on a single day in December, because it is. The correct trim triggers are an advisory committee announcement, a review-clock extension, or early fourth-quarter evidence that insurers are enforcing hard step-therapy through generic spironolactone across the class. The correct hold-through is a clean approval with a broad label, at which point the second question, whether a second mover can take share from AstraZeneca, becomes the whole thesis and deserves to be re-underwritten from scratch.
interrogator_dossier:
# Forensic Dossier - Mineralys Therapeutics, Inc. (MLYS)

**Event-driven special situation. Prepared 3 August 2026. Last close $25.52 (31 July 2026); market value about $2.25 billion on roughly 88.2 million shares.**

This is not a business-quality case. Mineralys has no product on the market and no revenue. The whole question is whether one dated regulatory event, the United States Food and Drug Administration's decision on its blood-pressure pill lorundrostat, due 22 December 2026 and now 141 days away, resolves favourably, what the shares are worth if it does, and what actually stops the fall if it does not.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Two years ago Mineralys told investors a platform story. Lorundrostat, a once-daily pill, blocks aldosterone synthase, the enzyme that makes aldosterone, the hormone that raises blood pressure and, over years, damages the heart and kidneys. Management framed that mechanism as something they could point at several diseases at once: hard-to-treat high blood pressure first, then chronic kidney disease, then obstructive sleep apnoea (the condition where breathing repeatedly stops during sleep).

That story has narrowed sharply, and the narrowing was forced rather than chosen.

- **The core indication delivered.** Two registrational studies, the Phase 3 Launch-HTN trial and the Phase 2 Advance-HTN trial, both showed clinically meaningful reductions in systolic blood pressure on top of existing therapy. Five positive Phase 2/3 trials in total sit behind the filing.
- **The second leg broke.** On 10 March 2026, in the same release that announced the regulator had accepted the filing, Mineralys disclosed that its Phase 2 Explore-OSA sleep-apnoea study missed its primary goal: evening-dosed lorundrostat produced no clinically meaningful improvement versus placebo on the apnoea-hypopnoea index (the standard count of breathing interruptions per hour). Blood pressure still fell handsomely in that population, but the sleep-apnoea indication is, for now, gone.
- **The kidney leg survived as a label argument, not a new market.** On 30 May 2026 at the European hypertension meeting, a post-hoc analysis of Launch-HTN showed significant blood-pressure reduction and reduced urinary albumin (a marker of kidney damage) in patients who also had chronic kidney disease. Useful ammunition for the label and for prescribers; not a separate approval. A further post-hoc proteomic analysis on heart-failure risk markers followed on 14 June 2026 at the endocrinology meeting, again supportive colour rather than a new indication.
- **A competitor got there first.** On 18 May 2026 the same agency approved AstraZeneca's baxdrostat, sold as Baxfendy, as the first aldosterone synthase inhibitor for adults with inadequately controlled high blood pressure, available from early June 2026. Mineralys is now definitively second to market in its own class, roughly seven months behind, against a company with a global cardiovascular sales force.

The net effect: what was sold as a multi-indication platform is now a single-drug, single-indication commercial launch into a market where a large rival is already detailing physicians.

## 2. CLAIMS versus THE NUMBERS (forensic)

| Management's claim | The evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Five positive clinical trials support the filing" | Filing accepted March 2026 on a standard review clock with a 22 December 2026 decision date, reconfirmed in the 6 May 2026 quarterly release and again in the 14 June 2026 conference release. No advisory committee meeting has been announced, so the agency has not signalled it needs outside help on the risk-benefit question. | Holds. The regulatory package is genuinely strong. |
| "Cash funds us into 2028" | $646.1 million of cash and investments at 31 March 2026, down only $10.5 million from $656.6 million at year-end 2025, because interest income and a lighter research bill offset most of the loss. Zero debt at that date. | Holds, and the balance sheet was reinforced in June. |
| "The royalty repurchase strengthens the balance sheet" | On 3 June 2026 the company paid Tanabe $200 million upfront to extinguish the royalty on lorundrostat and secure assignment of the related patents, funded with $150 million of new stock at $26.50 a share and $100 million drawn on a new senior secured loan from Pharmakon of up to $500 million. | Mixed. It removes a permanent revenue tax and buys the underlying intellectual property outright, a real and lasting gain. But it converted a contingent obligation into cash out the door plus first-ranking debt, and diluted holders by about 6.4% at a depressed price. |
| Cost discipline | Research spending fell to $24.4 million in the first quarter of 2026 from $37.9 million a year earlier, while general and administrative spending more than tripled to $21.0 million from $6.6 million. Quarterly net loss $39.3 million; trailing twelve-month net loss about $151.8 million. | Consistent with a company shifting from trials to launch preparation. The commercial build is real money spent before a single prescription exists. |

The financing structure is what defines the downside, so read it closely. The Pharmakon facility is a **senior secured** term loan of up to $500 million across four tranches, $100 million funded at closing, maturing June 2031, priced at the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (with a 3.25% floor) plus a 5.50% margin. Senior secured means the lender's claim ranks ahead of shareholders on the company's assets, including its cash. Any "the cash pile is the floor" argument must subtract that debt first and must assume the remaining three tranches carry drawdown conditions the company would likely fail in a rejection scenario.

There are also up to $265 million of commercial milestone payments still owed to Tanabe over time, $100 million newly agreed plus $165 million pre-existing. Those trigger only on commercial success, so they are a tax on the good outcome rather than a risk in the bad one, but they must be netted out of any launch valuation.

Pro-forma arithmetic for the balance sheet as it stands today: roughly $646 million at 31 March, less a quarter's burn of about $40 million, plus roughly $141 million net from the June share sale and $100 million drawn on the loan, less the $200 million paid to Tanabe, gives about $647 million of gross cash. Subtract the $100 million of senior secured debt and net cash is roughly $547 million, or about $6.20 a share, which is 24% of the current price.

## 3. TONE AND CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Rising on regulation, defensive on commerce. Management's language around the filing is precise and unhedged: a firm date, a defined package, no mention of information requests or review extensions. Its language around the competitive setup has become noticeably more conditional, shifting from "first in a new class" to arguments about label breadth, the kidney subgroup and market access.

The most informative signal is not verbal. In June, with the shares near a low, the board chose to spend $200 million of hard cash and take on secured debt to buy out a royalty on a drug that is not yet approved. Companies that doubt an approval do not do that. It is the single most credible statement of internal confidence in the file.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

High on timelines, unproven on commerce. Mineralys has hit every stated regulatory milestone: trials read out, filing submitted, filing accepted, decision date assigned and unchanged since March 2026. Cash guidance has held. The company funded itself well ahead of the event rather than into it, a discipline many small biotechs fail.

What has never been tested is commercial delivery. Nobody at Mineralys has sold this drug to a payer or a cardiologist. Every revenue figure in every analyst model is a forecast with no observed data behind it.

Reliability: **High** on process, **Untested** on launch.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three questions recur and none has a satisfying answer yet.

1. **Differentiation versus baxdrostat.** Sell-side opinion is genuinely split, and it has been moving in both directions. Goldman Sachs cut its target to $42 from $49 while keeping a buy rating; Bank of America raised its target to $43 from $38, also a buy. The published consensus target sits near $49 across roughly ten analysts, against a $25.52 price. Bulls size the aldosterone-synthase market above $5 billion and assume a roughly even split; bears argue lorundrostat is undifferentiated and structurally disadvantaged in the kidney-disease and SGLT2-combination opportunity where AstraZeneca has more to work with. Management leans on the kidney subgroup, which is post-hoc.
2. **Payer step-therapy.** Both drugs are add-ons to existing therapy, and insurers will very likely force patients through cheap generic spironolactone, a decades-old drug that also blunts aldosterone, before paying for either. Management has not addressed this directly in public materials.
3. **Who pays for the launch.** A branded cardiovascular launch against AstraZeneca is expensive. The undrawn $400 million of the Pharmakon facility and future equity are the visible answers; neither is free.

## 6. RED FLAGS AND GREEN FLAGS

**Concerning**
- The sleep-apnoea miss was disclosed on the same day as the good news about filing acceptance (10 March 2026). Burying a miss under a beat is a disclosure choice, not an accident.
- Senior secured debt now ranks ahead of shareholders on the cash. That materially weakens the "cash is the floor" argument.
- Short interest remains high at 9.55 million shares, about 14.3% of the freely traded stock, as of the 15 July 2026 settlement, needing about 9.8 days of average volume to cover.
- The shares are down about 46% from the 52-week high of $47.65 and drifted lower again in late July, to $25.52 from $26.71 a week earlier. The tape is not confirming the bull case.

**Positive**
- The decision date has not moved and no advisory committee has been called. The two classic tells of a troubled review are both absent, and their absence carries more weight the later it gets in a standard review.
- A rival drug with the same mechanism was approved by the same agency on 18 May 2026. The regulator has already accepted the mechanism, the blood-pressure endpoint and the safety management, chiefly the risk of high potassium and low sodium. That is meaningful de-risking of the approval itself, even as it worsens the commercial picture.
- The royalty buyout means Mineralys keeps 100% of future economics and will own the underlying patents outright, precisely the housekeeping a board does when it wants maximum value from a launch or from a sale of the company.
- Roughly $647 million of gross cash against $100 million of drawn debt, with funding secured well before the event.
- Short interest is now falling, not rising: the 15 July reading was down about 14% from the prior settlement, reversing the spring trend and a small but real change from our late-July read.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The vocabulary has shifted from "platform" and "comorbidities" to "label" and "access." That is the language of a company preparing to fight for share, not one expecting to define a category.

The sequencing of the June transactions is telling. Buying the royalty before approval, at a depressed share price, costs more in dilution than waiting would have. Doing it anyway implies either high internal confidence in the December decision, or a wish to have a clean, wholly-owned asset ready for a strategic conversation, or both. Either reading is constructive.

The company has also kept hiring: a routine equity-inducement filing on 27 July 2026 granted options and restricted stock to new non-executive employees. Small in itself, but consistent with a commercial build continuing on schedule rather than a company hedging against a bad outcome.

Finally, sleep apnoea stopped appearing as a value driver in the script after March. Growth drivers that quietly disappear rarely come back.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE. The event is on schedule and fully funded; the commercial story around it has narrowed.**

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing this: **the approval and the payoff have come apart.** Because a competitor with the identical mechanism was approved in May, the probability that lorundrostat is approved on 22 December has gone up, and the value of that approval has gone down. The market understands this. It is why the shares fell roughly 25% in six sessions in early June and now sit at $25.52 against a street consensus target near $49.

The practical consequence is that this is not a classic wide-spread event trade where a doubtful approval is being mispriced. It is a mildly negatively-skewed binary: roughly a nine-in-ten chance of an outcome that is largely expected and worth perhaps a 30% to 50% re-rate, against roughly a one-in-ten chance of a rejection letter that would likely halve the shares.

And the floor is soft. Netting the drawn senior secured loan against roughly $647 million of cash leaves about $6.20 a share of net cash, 24% of the current price, and it sits behind the lender. Realistic support in a rejection is not cash but the residual worth of a re-fileable drug with two positive registrational trials in a class the agency has already approved: call it $13, roughly where the shares traded a year ago at $12.59 before the pivotal data. That is an estimate, not a contractual backstop, and the director should size the position as though half the capital is genuinely at risk on a single day.

**Economic moat: none that can yet be evidenced.** No revenues, no margins, no returns to measure. What exists is patent exclusivity on a molecule the company will shortly own outright, real protection but of an unproven franchise, entering a market where a large competitor is already selling and where cheap generics anchor what insurers will pay. The structural pressure worth naming is reimbursement: payers will push patients through generic spironolactone first, compressing both price and volume for the whole class. That is a manageable headwind on the size of the prize, not a terminal threat to the asset's existence.

bull_thesis:
The bull case is that a dated, well-supported regulatory decision on 22 December 2026 converts Mineralys from a speculative clinical-stage company into the owner of a commercial cardiovascular drug, and that the market has already marked the shares down for the wrong reason.

Start with the event itself. The United States Food and Drug Administration accepted the filing for lorundrostat in March 2026 and set a decision date of 22 December 2026. That date has not moved. No advisory committee meeting has been called, which is normally a sign the agency does not think it needs outside help with the risk-benefit question. The filing rests on two registrational studies, the Phase 3 Launch-HTN trial and the Phase 2 Advance-HTN trial, both showing clinically meaningful reductions in systolic blood pressure on top of existing therapy, within a body of five completed successful Phase 2/3 trials.

The strongest single piece of evidence for approval is external. On 15 May 2026 the same agency approved AstraZeneca's baxdrostat, sold as Baxfendy, as the first aldosterone synthase inhibitor for adults with uncontrolled high blood pressure. Aldosterone synthase is the enzyme that makes aldosterone, the hormone that raises blood pressure and damages the heart and kidneys over time; lorundrostat blocks the same enzyme. The regulator has therefore already accepted the mechanism, the blood-pressure endpoint and the safety management that goes with it. A second entrant with two positive registrational trials into a class the agency has just blessed is about as de-risked as a first approval gets. A reasonable probability of approval is around 90%.

The second pillar is that management has voted with real money. On 3 June 2026 Mineralys paid Tanabe $200 million in cash to extinguish the royalty on lorundrostat and to secure assignment of the related patents, funding it with $150 million of stock sold at $26.50 a share and $100 million drawn from a new senior secured loan facility of up to $500 million from Pharmakon. The third pillar is the size of the prize relative to what is priced. Wainwright, with a consensus near $49 against a live price of $26.71. And most importantly, on 15 May 2026 the same agency approved AstraZeneca's baxdrostat, which blocks the identical enzyme for the identical patients — meaning the regulator has already accepted the mechanism, the endpoint and the safety profile of this class. A second entrant into a freshly validated class, with a clean review and no committee, is about a nine-in-ten proposition.

Management has staked real money on the same view. In June it paid Tanabe $200 million cash to extinguish the royalty on a drug that is not yet approved and to take assignment of the patents, funded with $150 million of stock at $26.50 and $100 million of a new $500 million senior secured facility. Nobody does that at a depressed price if they expect a rejection letter. It also leaves Mineralys, on 23 December, as a wholly-owned, approved, single-asset cardiovascular company — the cleanest acquisition target imaginable in a class a major pharmaceutical company has just proven out.

And the price has been washed out for reasons that are only half about the fundamentals. The shares are $26.71, down about 44% from a 52-week high of $47.65, below both the 50-day and 200-day averages, with about 14.4% of the free float sold short. Some of that decline is legitimate — the sleep-apnoea study failed its primary endpoint in March, which killed the platform story. Some of it is mechanical — a forced 6.4% equity issue in June into a falling tape. Against a street consensus target near $49, with refreshed post-selloff targets from $42 to $56, the gap is real.

Now the honest part. Two of the three legs a top-conviction event trade requires are here; the third is not.

First, the payoff is negatively skewed. Because the competitor was approved in May, the approval is expected — and expected events do not pay much. A clean approval is worth perhaps a 30% to 40% move, to roughly $38, not to the $49 consensus, which is a twelve-month launch valuation requiring commercial proof that will not exist until deep into 2027. A rejection letter roughly halves the stock. So the shape is +42% against -51%, about 0.8 to 1. It is the odds that make this work — 0.90 x $38 plus 0.10 x $13 gives a base-case value near $35.50, or +33% from here — not the ratio.

Second, and this is the binding constraint, the downside floor is soft. There is no deal price, no contractual payout, no cash backstop near the market. Gross cash of roughly $640 million looks like protection until you note the Pharmakon loan is senior secured — the lender ranks ahead of shareholders on the company's assets, including that cash — and that the remaining three tranches carry conditions a rejected company would fail. Net cash is about $6.15 a share, just 23% of the price. The realistic $13 support level is our estimate of where a re-fileable asset in an already-approved class would clear, corroborated only by where the stock traded a year ago before the pivotal data. That is a judgement, not a floor, and it is why the margin-of-safety score is a two while the event score is a four.

The timing call: enter now rather than waiting. The reason is asymmetric information flow between here and December. The two things that would break the thesis — an advisory committee being called or the review clock being extended — get less likely with every week that passes this late in a standard review, while the reward for owning the position does not improve by waiting. Second-quarter results on 11 August will show a widening loss and a heavier commercial build, which may offer a slightly better entry, but that is a coin-flip against the risk of the shorts starting to cover into the autumn.

Size it accordingly: a full-conviction thesis at half-conviction size. Underwrite as though roughly half the capital is genuinely at risk on a single day in December, because it is. The correct trim triggers are an advisory committee announcement, a review-clock extension, or early fourth-quarter evidence that insurers are enforcing hard step-therapy through generic spironolactone across the class. The correct hold-through is a clean approval with a broad label — at which point the second question, whether a second-mover can take share from AstraZeneca, becomes the whole thesis and deserves to be re-underwritten from scratch.

# Forensic Dossier — Mineralys Therapeutics, Inc. (MLYS)

**Event-driven special situation. Prepared 27 July 2026. Live price $26.71; market value about $2.35 billion on roughly 88.2 million shares.**

This is not a business-quality case. Mineralys has no product on the market and no revenue. The entire question is whether a single, dated regulatory event — the United States Food and Drug Administration's decision on its blood-pressure pill, due 22 December 2026 — resolves favourably, what the shares are worth if it does, and what actually stops the fall if it does not.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story Mineralys told investors two years ago was a platform story. Lorundrostat, its once-daily pill, blocks aldosterone synthase — the enzyme that makes aldosterone, a hormone that raises blood pressure and, over time, damages the heart and kidneys. Management framed this as a mechanism that could be pointed at several diseases at once: hard-to-treat high blood pressure first, then chronic kidney disease, then obstructive sleep apnoea (the condition where breathing repeatedly stops during sleep).

That story has narrowed sharply, and the narrowing has been forced rather than chosen.

- **The core indication delivered.** Two registrational trials — the Phase 3 Launch-HTN study and the Phase 2 Advance-HTN study — both showed clinically meaningful reductions in systolic blood pressure on top of existing therapy. The company has now completed five successful Phase 2/3 trials in total. The regulatory filing rests on this body of work.
- **The second leg broke.** On 10 March 2026, alongside the announcement that the FDA had accepted the filing, Mineralys disclosed that its Phase 2 Explore-OSA sleep-apnoea study missed its primary goal: evening-dosed lorundrostat did not produce a clinically meaningful improvement versus placebo on the apnoea-hypopnoea index (the standard count of breathing interruptions per hour). Blood pressure still fell handsomely in that population — 11.1 mmHg from baseline, 6.2 mmHg placebo-adjusted — but the sleep-apnoea indication itself is, for now, gone.
- **The kidney leg survived as a label argument, not a new market.** At the European hypertension meeting on 30 May 2026, a post-hoc analysis of Launch-HTN showed significant blood-pressure reduction and reduced urine albumin (a marker of kidney damage) in patients who also had chronic kidney disease. That is useful commercial ammunition for the label and for prescribers. It is not a separate approval.
- **A competitor got there first.** On 15 May 2026 the FDA approved AstraZeneca's baxdrostat, marketed as Baxfendy, as the first aldosterone synthase inhibitor for adults with uncontrolled high blood pressure, available from early June 2026. Mineralys is now, definitively, second to market in its own class, roughly seven months behind, against a competitor with a global sales force.

The net effect: what was sold as a multi-indication platform is now a single-drug, single-indication commercial launch into a market where a large rival is already detailing physicians.

## 2. CLAIMS versus THE NUMBERS (forensic)

| Management's claim | The evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Five positive clinical trials support the filing" | Filing accepted by the FDA in March 2026 with a standard review clock and a 22 December 2026 decision date. No advisory committee meeting has been announced — the agency has not signalled it needs outside help on the risk-benefit question. | Holds. The regulatory package is genuinely strong. |
| "Cash funds us into 2028" | $646.1 million in cash and investments at 31 March 2026, down only $10.5 million from $656.6 million at year-end 2025, because $6.0 million of interest income and a lighter research bill offset the loss. | Holds, and the balance was strengthened further in June. |
| "The royalty repurchase strengthens the balance sheet" | Partly true and partly spin. On 3 June 2026 the company paid Tanabe $200 million upfront to extinguish the royalty on lorundrostat and secure assignment of the related patents, funded by $150 million of new stock at $26.50 a share and $100 million drawn on a new senior secured loan. | Mixed. It removes a permanent revenue tax and buys the underlying intellectual property — a real, lasting gain. But it converted a contingent obligation into cash out the door plus first-ranking debt, and it diluted holders by about 6.4% at a depressed price. |
| Cost discipline | Research spending fell to $24.4 million in the first quarter of 2026 from $37.9 million a year earlier, while general and administrative spending more than tripled to $21.0 million from $6.6 million. Quarterly net loss $39.3 million. | Consistent with a company shifting from trials to launch preparation. The commercial build is real money being spent before a single prescription exists. |

The financing structure deserves close reading, because it is what defines the downside. The Pharmakon facility is a **senior secured** term loan of up to $500 million across four tranches, $100 million funded at closing, maturing June 2031, priced at the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (with a 3.25% floor) plus a 5.50% margin — call it high-single-digit to low-double-digit interest. Senior secured means the lender's claim ranks ahead of shareholders on the company's assets, including its cash. Any calculation of "the shares are backstopped by the cash pile" must subtract that debt first, and must assume the remaining three tranches carry drawdown conditions the company may not meet in a bad scenario.

There are also up to $265 million of commercial milestone payments still owed to Tanabe over time — $100 million newly agreed plus $165 million pre-existing. Those only trigger on commercial success, so they are a tax on the good outcome, not a risk in the bad one, but they must be netted out of any launch valuation.

## 3. TONE AND CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

Rising on regulation, defensive on commerce. Management's language around the filing is precise and unhedged — a firm date, a defined package, no talk of information requests or review extensions. Management's language around the competitive setup has become noticeably more conditional: the pitch has shifted from "first in a new class" to arguments about label breadth, the kidney-disease subgroup, and market access.

The most informative signal is not verbal. In June, with the shares near a low, the board chose to spend $200 million of hard cash and take on secured debt to buy out a royalty on a drug that is not yet approved. Companies that doubt an approval do not do that. It is the single most credible statement of internal confidence in the file.

Against that, one governance detail cuts the other way: a roughly $350,000 insider sale in June 2026, reported ahead of the December decision. Small in absolute terms and likely routine, but worth noting when the whole thesis is a binary event.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

High on timelines, unproven on commerce. Mineralys has hit its stated regulatory milestones: trials read out, filing submitted, filing accepted, decision date assigned and unchanged since March. Cash guidance has held. The company has funded itself well ahead of the event rather than into it — a discipline many small biotechs fail.

What has never been tested is commercial delivery. Nobody at Mineralys has sold this drug to a payer or a cardiologist. Every revenue figure in every analyst model is a forecast with no observed data behind it.

Reliability: **High** on process, **Untested** on launch.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three questions recur and none has a satisfying answer yet.

1. **Differentiation versus baxdrostat.** Sell-side opinion is genuinely split. TD Cowen's Tara Bancroft sizes the aldosterone-synthase market at more than $5 billion, expects an even split between the two drugs, and argues Mineralys wins on label and pricing. Bearish commentary argues lorundrostat is undifferentiated and structurally disadvantaged in the kidney-disease and SGLT2-combination opportunity where AstraZeneca has more to work with. Management's answer leans on the kidney subgroup data, which is post-hoc.
2. **Payer step-therapy.** Both drugs must be prescribed on top of existing therapy, and insurers will very likely force patients through cheap generic spironolactone — a decades-old drug that also blocks aldosterone's effects — before paying for either. Management has not addressed this directly in public materials.
3. **Who pays for the launch.** A branded cardiovascular launch against AstraZeneca is expensive. The undrawn $400 million of the Pharmakon facility and future equity are the visible answers; neither is free.

## 6. RED FLAGS AND GREEN FLAGS

**Concerning**
- The sleep-apnoea failure was disclosed on the same day as the good news about the filing acceptance (10 March 2026). Burying a miss under a beat is a disclosure choice, not an accident.
- Senior secured debt now sits ahead of shareholders on the cash. That materially weakens the "cash is the floor" argument.
- Short interest is elevated at roughly 14.4% of the freely traded shares and has risen about 22% over the past year. Somebody is positioned for the bad outcome.
- The shares are down about 44% from the 52-week high of $47.65 and trade below both the 50-day (about $27.03) and 200-day (about $31.87) averages. The tape is not confirming the bull case.

**Positive**
- The decision date has not moved and no advisory committee has been called — the two classic tells of a troubled review are both absent.
- A rival drug with the same mechanism was approved by the same agency nine weeks ago. The FDA has already blessed the mechanism, the endpoint and the safety management. That is meaningful de-risking of the approval itself, even as it worsens the commercial picture.
- The royalty buyout means Mineralys keeps 100% of future economics and will own the underlying patents outright — precisely the housekeeping a board does when it wants maximum value from a launch or from a sale of the company.
- Roughly $640 million of gross cash against about $100 million of drawn debt, with funding secured well before the event.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The vocabulary has shifted from "platform" and "comorbidities" to "label" and "access." That is the language of a company preparing to fight for share, not one expecting to define a category.

Second, the sequencing of the June transactions is telling. Buying the royalty *before* approval, at a depressed share price, costs more in dilution than waiting would have. Doing it anyway implies either high internal confidence in the December decision, or a desire to have a clean, wholly-owned asset available for a strategic conversation — or both. Either reading is constructive.

Third, the company's own guidance language stopped referencing sleep apnoea as a value driver after March. Growth drivers that quietly disappear from the script rarely come back.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE — the event is on schedule and fully funded; the commercial story around it has narrowed.**

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing this: **the approval and the payoff have come apart.** Because a competitor with the identical mechanism was approved in May, the probability that lorundrostat is approved on 22 December has gone *up* — and the value of that approval has gone *down*. The market understands this. That is why the shares fell roughly 25% in six sessions in early June and now sit at $26.71 against a street consensus target near $49.

The practical consequence is that this is not a classic wide-spread event trade where a doubtful approval is being mispriced. It is a negatively-skewed binary: roughly a nine-in-ten chance of an outcome that is largely expected and worth perhaps a 30% to 40% re-rate, against roughly a one-in-ten chance of a rejection letter that would likely halve the shares. The expected value is clearly positive, but it is carried by the odds, not by the shape of the payoff.

And the floor is soft. Netting the drawn senior secured loan against roughly $640 million of cash leaves about $6.15 a share of net cash — only 23% of the current price, and it sits behind the lender. The realistic support in a rejection scenario is not cash but the residual worth of a re-fileable drug with two positive registrational trials in an already-approved class: call it $13, which is roughly where the shares traded a year ago at $12.59 before the pivotal data. That is an estimate, not a contractual backstop, and the director should size the position as though half the capital is genuinely at risk.

**Economic moat: none that can yet be evidenced.** There are no revenues, no margins and no returns to measure. What exists is patent exclusivity on a molecule the company will shortly own outright — real protection, but protection of an unproven commercial franchise, and one entering a market where a large competitor is already selling and where cheap generic alternatives anchor what insurers will pay. The structural pressure worth naming is reimbursement: payers will push patients through generic spironolactone first, which compresses both price and volume for the whole class. That is a manageable headwind on the size of the prize, not a terminal threat to the asset's existence.
